stem:
A 26-year-old whose last period was six weeks ago presents to a regional emergency department with lower abdominal pain and right shoulder-tip pain; she fainted at home. Her pulse is 124 beats/min and blood pressure 104/68 mmHg lying, falling to 84/52 mmHg on sitting. Her abdomen is tender with guarding. Urine hCG is positive and serum hCG is 1,800 IU/L. The formal pelvic ultrasound list opens tomorrow morning.

What should the gynaecology registrar arrange?

options.label: A
options.text: Intramuscular methotrexate, as her hCG is in the range it treats
options.explanation: Methotrexate needs haemodynamic stability and no sign of rupture; a low hCG does not make it safe in a woman with a postural drop and peritonism.

options.label: B
options.text: Repeat serum hCG in 48 hours to confirm an abnormal pregnancy
options.explanation: Serial hCG is for stable women on the unknown-location pathway; waiting 48 hours with suspected rupture risks exsanguination.

options.label: C
options.text: Admission for observation until tomorrow's formal pelvic ultrasound
options.explanation: A postural drop, shoulder-tip pain and guarding point to intraperitoneal bleeding, so observation overnight delays haemorrhage control.

options.label: D
options.text: Resuscitation and surgery in theatre today, without awaiting the scan
options.explanation: A positive pregnancy test with syncope, a postural drop, shoulder-tip pain and peritonism is a ruptured ectopic until proven otherwise: resuscitate and operate without waiting for imaging.

options.label: E
options.text: CT of the abdomen and pelvis to confirm haemoperitoneum before theatre
options.explanation: CT delays theatre and adds radiation. The clinical picture is enough, and a bedside scan can be done without holding up surgery.

context: Compensated shock (tachycardia with a postural drop) plus shoulder-tip pain and peritonism in early pregnancy means a ruptured ectopic: resuscitate and operate, whatever the hCG.
